whohe1-all-of-them-the-rule-the-line-and.reason: Opens on the curriculum request and Luke 24; the yes (one rule, kept the same, found 669 passages) comes in movements two and three; ends on the twenty edge passages awaiting the elders.
whohe1-all-of-them-the-rule-the-line-and.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Could one written rule find Him in 669 passages? Yes. One rule, kept the same everywhere, brought in every scene of the four Gospels and Revelation, every New Testament passage that names Him, and every Old Testament passage the New Testament quotes of Him or says pictured or held Him. A machine ran it over every verse, and each quotation match was judged by hand. That is why anyone can check the count.
whohe1-all-of-them-the-rule-the-line-and.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Could one written rule find Him across the Word? It did: six hundred and sixty-nine passages, five hundred and ninety-five in the New Testament and seventy-four in the Old, each placed on the line and showing what it calls Him. Where the New Testament does not speak, the lesson does not guess; twenty passages wait for the elders' word. This is how He read the Word Himself, beginning at Moses (Luke 24:27). Every passage points to one Person: Jesus, the Lamb of Yahweh and the Eternal Son of Yahweh.

teen.open: Can one simple rule find every passage about Jesus in the Bible? Yes. One rule, used the same way everywhere, found 669 of them.
teen.close: So the rule works, and anyone can check it. Jesus opened the Scriptures this way Himself, and every one of those passages points to Him.

senior.open: The title asks whether one written rule could find Him in 669 passages. It did, applied the same way to every verse, with each quotation match judged by hand and its reason recorded.
senior.close: So the count stands on a rule anyone can check, and it follows the way He Himself opened the Scriptures, beginning at Moses. Across the whole line one Person is shown: Jesus, the Lamb of Yahweh and the Eternal Son of Yahweh.

whohe2-before-time-and-the-beginning.reason: Movement one answers at once (In the beginning was the Word; glory with the Father before the world was) and the close lands it: the One born in Bethlehem was already the Maker and the Beloved of the Father.

whohe3-the-fathers-and-moses.reason: Answers in its first line (Jesus: Moses wrote of me), but ends on what the register does NOT hold (Joshua, Judges, Ruth) rather than landing the yes.
whohe3-the-fathers-and-moses.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Did Moses and Abraham really write about Jesus? Jesus said Moses did (John 5:46), and the New Testament shows where. The seed promised to Abraham is Christ (Galatians 3:16). The passover, the lifted serpent, the manna, and the rock all point to Him, and Moses foretold the Prophet like himself (Acts 3:22). Abraham received the promise and rejoiced to see His day (John 8:56). Sixteen passages, each checked by the New Testament's own words, give one answer: yes, these books speak of Him.

teen.open: Did Moses really write about Jesus? Jesus said he did, and the New Testament shows exactly where.
teen.close: So yes. The promise to Abraham, the passover lamb, the bread from heaven, and the rock all point to Jesus, and the New Testament says so in its own words.

senior.open: The title asks whether Moses and the fathers truly wrote of Jesus. Jesus Himself said Moses did, and the New Testament names each place.
senior.close: So the answer is yes, checked passage by passage against the New Testament's own words. Abraham's promised seed, the passover, the manna, the rock, and the Prophet like Moses all point to Him.

whohe4-the-kings-and-the-psalms.reason: Movement one answers (the throne established for ever; Paul names the Seed as Jesus), but the lesson ends on a register note about how psalms are marked.
whohe4-the-kings-and-the-psalms.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Did Yahweh promise a king whose throne never ends? He did, through Nathan to David: He would establish the kingdom of David's seed and its throne for ever (2 Samuel 7:12-13). Paul names that Seed: Jesus (Acts 13:23). David's songs call Him Son (Psalms 2:7) and David's own Lord, seated at the right hand (Psalms 110:1), and Hebrews says the throne that is for ever and ever is spoken to the Son (Hebrews 1:8). The promised King is Jesus, and His throne has no end.

teen.open: Did Yahweh promise David a King who would rule forever? Yes, and the New Testament says that King is Jesus.
teen.close: So the forever King from David's family is Jesus. David even called Him Lord, and He sits at the right hand.

senior.open: The title asks whether Yahweh promised a King whose throne would never end. He did, through the prophet Nathan to David, and the apostles name that King as Jesus.
senior.close: So the promise stands fulfilled. The Son of David whom David himself called Lord, seated at the right hand, is Jesus, and His throne is for ever and ever.

whohe5-the-prophets.reason: Opens with 1 Peter 1:11 (the Spirit of Christ testified beforehand), answering yes early; ends on the passage count and how undated prophets are marked.
whohe5-the-prophets.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Did the prophets really see Jesus coming? They did, and the New Testament shows it line by line. Isaiah foretold the virgin's Son and His wounds, Micah named Bethlehem, Zechariah saw the lowly King and the pierced One, and Daniel saw the Son of man coming with the clouds. The Spirit of Christ in them testified beforehand (1 Peter 1:11), and Isaiah saw His glory and spoke of Him (John 12:41). Across thirty-one passages, long before He came, they were seeing Him.

teen.open: Did the prophets really see Jesus coming long before He was born? Yes, and the New Testament quotes them to show it.
teen.close: So yes. They told of His birth in Bethlehem, His wounds, and His glory long ahead of time, and it all came true in Jesus.

senior.open: The title asks whether the prophets truly foresaw Jesus. They did; the Spirit of Christ in them testified beforehand of His sufferings and the glory to follow.
senior.close: So the answer is yes. His birth, His titles, His wounds, and His glory were written long before He came, and the New Testament names each fulfillment in Jesus.

whohe6-he-comes-in-the-flesh.reason: Opens with Galatians 4:4 and John 1:14 (the Son sent, the Word made flesh), but ends on the register count instead of landing who was coming.
whohe6-he-comes-in-the-flesh.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Before the manger, who was already coming? The Son, sent by the Father in the fulness of time (Galatians 4:4), the Word made flesh (John 1:14). He was named JESUS before He was conceived, because He would save His people from their sins (Matthew 1:21), and Elisabeth called Him Lord while He was still in His mother's womb (Luke 1:43). Born in Bethlehem, a Saviour, Christ the Lord (Luke 2:11), at twelve He was already about His Father's business (Luke 2:49).

teen.open: Who was coming before Jesus was born? The Son of Yahweh, sent by the Father at just the right time.
teen.close: So the baby in the manger was already the Son. He was named Jesus before He was born, called Lord before His birth, and at twelve He was in His Father's house.

senior.open: The title asks who was already coming before the manger. The Word answers: the Son, sent forth by the Father in the fulness of time and made flesh to dwell among us.
senior.close: So the One who came was the Son of the Father, named before His conception, confessed as Lord while yet unborn, and at twelve already about His Father's business.

whohe7-his-ministry-every-scene.reason: Opens only by saying every scene is included; who He is emerges scattered across four movements of quotations and is never drawn together; ends on the register.
whohe7-his-ministry-every-scene.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Can the Gospels show who Jesus really is, scene by scene? Yes. Each Gospel says its whole book is about Him, so every scene counts. Across them four witnesses give one answer: the Father calls Him His beloved Son, Jesus says He is the light of the world and the resurrection, Peter confesses Him the Christ, and His works show He has power to forgive sins.
whohe7-his-ministry-every-scene.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Could the Gospels show who Jesus really is? Scene by scene, they do. The Father's voice at the Jordan, His own words in the synagogue and the temple, Peter's confession, "Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God", and even the wind and the sea that obey Him all say the same thing. Two hundred and eight scenes, one answer: He is the beloved Son, the Christ, with power on earth to forgive sins.

teen.open: Can the Gospels really show us who Jesus is? Yes. Every scene adds to the answer.
teen.close: So scene after scene, the answer is the same: Jesus is the Father's beloved Son and the Christ, and even the wind and the sea obey Him.

senior.open: The title asks whether the Gospels, scene by scene, can show who Jesus truly is. They can, for the Father, Jesus Himself, His followers, and His works all bear the same witness.
senior.close: So across two hundred and eight scenes the witness agrees: He is the beloved Son of the Father, the Christ, with power on earth to forgive sins.

whohe8-the-cross.reason: Says He spoke plainly but not what He said; the answer is spread across five movements of quotations and never summed up; ends on the register count.
whohe8-the-cross.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. In His final hours, what did Jesus say about who He is? More plainly than ever: He is Master and Lord, the way, the truth, and the life, the one in whom the Father is seen. Asked if He was the Christ, the Son of the Blessed, He answered, "I am". And on the cross He said the work was finished. Here are the five moments.
whohe8-the-cross.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. What did Jesus say about who He is in His final hours? In the upper room, that He is Lord and the only way to the Father. In the garden, "I am he", and the soldiers fell back. Before the council, that He is the Christ who will sit at the right hand of power. On the cross, that the work is finished. And a Roman centurion, watching, said it too: "Truly this was the Son of God".

teen.open: What did Jesus say about Himself in His last hours? He said it plainly: He is Lord, the way to the Father, and the Christ.
teen.close: So right up to the cross, Jesus told the truth about who He is. He finished the work, and even a Roman soldier watching said, "Truly this was the Son of God".

senior.open: The title asks what Jesus said of Himself in His final hours. He spoke more plainly than at any other time: Master and Lord, the way to the Father, the Christ who would sit at the right hand of power.
senior.close: So from the upper room to the cross He bore witness to the truth about Himself and declared the work finished. The centurion who watched Him die confessed it as well.

whohe10-his-witnesses-in-acts.reason: Opens with Acts 1:8 only; what the witnesses said (Lord and Christ, no other name, Lord of all, Judge, still seen) is spread across movements and never gathered; ends on the register.
whohe10-his-witnesses-in-acts.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Who did the first witnesses say Jesus is? Lord and Christ (Acts 2:36), the one name by which we must be saved (Acts 4:12), Lord of all, and the Judge of the living and the dead (Acts 10:36, 42). And He was still seen and heard: Stephen saw Him standing at the right hand, and on the Damascus road Saul heard Him speak.
whohe10-his-witnesses-in-acts.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Who did the first witnesses say He is? From Jerusalem to Athens they said the same thing. Jesus, the one who was crucified, is Lord and Christ. There is salvation in no other name. He is Lord of all and the Judge of the world, and His rising from the dead is the assurance (Acts 17:31). And He is not absent: Stephen saw Him at the right hand, and Saul heard Him say, "I am Jesus whom thou persecutest".

teen.open: What did the first Christians say about Jesus? That He is Lord, the only name that saves, and the Judge of everyone.
teen.close: So the first witnesses were clear. Jesus is Lord of all and will judge the world, and Stephen saw Him and Saul heard Him, alive at the right hand.

senior.open: The title asks what the first witnesses declared about Jesus. In Acts they named Him Lord and Christ, the only name given for salvation, Lord of all, and the appointed Judge.
senior.close: So their witness was one and steady: the crucified Jesus is Lord and Christ, Saviour and Judge, raised from the dead, and still seen and heard at the right hand.

whohe9-he-is-risen-and-he-goes-up.reason: Movement one answers at once (He is not here: for He is risen), but the lesson ends on the register count, not on the risen and ascended Lord.
whohe9-he-is-risen-and-he-goes-up.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Did the tomb stay closed? No. The angel said, "He is not here: for he is risen, as he said". He showed His hands and feet to be handled, Thomas answered, "My Lord and my God", and He was seen for forty days, once by more than five hundred at once (1 Corinthians 15:6). Then He was carried up into heaven and sat at the right hand, and He will come again as He went (Acts 1:11).

teen.open: Did Jesus stay in the tomb? No. He rose, showed Himself alive, and then went up to heaven.
teen.close: So the tomb is empty. Jesus is alive, hundreds saw Him, He went up into heaven, and He is coming back the same way.

senior.open: The title asks whether the tomb stayed closed. It did not: on the first day of the week the angel told the women He was risen, as He said.
senior.close: So the answer is plain. He rose bodily, was seen by many witnesses over forty days, was taken up into heaven, and sits at the right hand, from where He will come again as He went.

whohe11-the-letters-who-he-is-to-the-chu.reason: Movement one answers at once (Colossians 1:15, Christ the image of the invisible God), but the lesson ends on how the register records writers and readers.
whohe11-the-letters-who-he-is-to-the-chu.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Who is the image of the invisible Yahweh? Jesus Christ. The letters say so in sentences the whole church has confessed: by Him all things were created and in Him they consist (Colossians 1:16-17), in Him dwells all the fulness of the Godhead bodily (Colossians 2:9), and He is the brightness of the Father's glory (Hebrews 1:3). He humbled Himself to the cross and was given the name above every name. Of the Son, John writes, "This is the true God, and eternal life".

teen.open: Who shows us what the invisible Yahweh is like? Jesus. Paul calls Him "the image of the invisible God".
teen.close: So when you want to know what Yahweh is like, look at Jesus. He made all things, holds them together, and every knee will bow to Him.

senior.open: The title asks who is the image of the invisible Yahweh. The letters answer at once: Jesus Christ, in whom all the fulness of the Godhead dwells bodily.
senior.close: So the answer the churches have confessed from the start is Jesus Christ: Creator and sustainer of all things, humbled to the cross and exalted above every name, the one Mediator, the true and eternal life.

whohe13-he-comes-again.reason: Opens on 'no date'; the answer (Acts 1:11, this same Jesus in like manner) comes in Movement One, but it ends on the register count and confession, not on the return itself.
whohe13-he-comes-again.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Will Jesus, who was taken up into heaven, come back the same way? Yes. On the mount called Olivet, two men in white told the disciples that this same Jesus will come in like manner as they saw Him go (Acts 1:11). The Word gives no date, and we give none. But forty-nine passages, from every era of the line, point to that day.
whohe13-he-comes-again.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Gone into heaven, coming back the same way? Yes, and the Word says it again and again. The same Jesus who went up from Olivet will come in the clouds with power and great glory (Acts 1:11; Matthew 24:30). He promised it Himself (John 14:3). Every eye will see Him (Revelation 1:7), the dead in Christ will rise first (1 Thessalonians 4:16), and He comes with salvation completed and His reward with Him (Hebrews 9:28; Revelation 22:12). No date is given. The promise is.

teen.open: Jesus went up into heaven. Will He come back the same way? Yes. The Word says this same Jesus will come again just as He went (Acts 1:11).
teen.close: So the answer is yes. The same Jesus is coming back, every eye will see Him, and He promised to receive His own to be where He is (John 14:3).

senior.open: The title asks whether Jesus, taken up into heaven, will return in the same way. The two men in white at Olivet answered it plainly: this same Jesus will come in like manner (Acts 1:11).
senior.close: So the question has its answer across the whole line of Scripture. The same Jesus will return, seen by every eye, raising the dead in Christ and completing salvation. No date is given; forty-nine passages give the promise.

whohe12-the-revelation-of-jesus-christ.reason: First sentence answers (the book names its subject: the Revelation of Jesus Christ, 1:1), but it ends on the register's marking scheme and the confession rather than landing that answer.
whohe12-the-revelation-of-jesus-christ.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. What does the last book reveal first? Jesus Christ Himself. Its very first words name Him as its subject (Revelation 1:1). Then the book shows Him: the faithful witness who loved us and washed us from our sins in His own blood, the One who was dead and is alive for evermore with the keys of hell and of death, the Lamb who was slain and is worthy, and the King of kings and Lord of lords. Before anything else in Revelation, you meet Him.

teen.open: The last book of the Bible tells you right away what it is about: Jesus Christ (Revelation 1:1). Before anything else, it shows you Him.
teen.close: So what does Revelation reveal first? Jesus. The faithful witness, the Lamb who was slain and now lives forever, the King of kings. Meet Him first, and the rest of the book makes sense.

senior.open: The title asks what the last book of the Word reveals first. Its opening verse answers: it is the Revelation of Jesus Christ (Revelation 1:1). He is the subject before anything else is shown.
senior.close: So the last book reveals its Lord before it reveals any event: the faithful witness, the One alive for evermore, the worthy Lamb, the King of kings and Lord of lords. Everything else in it is seen in His light.

whohe14-for-ever.reason: The answer (Jesus, the same for ever, with an endless reign, priesthood and worship) is implied by the movements but never said plainly; the title's 'What never runs out?' is not named or landed.
whohe14-for-ever.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. What never runs out? Jesus Christ, and all that is His. He is the same yesterday, today, and for ever (Hebrews 13:8). His kingdom has no end, His priesthood is unchangeable, and the worship of the Lamb goes on for ever and ever. The line of the Word began before time with Him, and it ends in for ever with Him.
whohe14-for-ever.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. What never runs out? He does, and everything that is His. His reign has no end (Luke 1:33; Revelation 11:15). His priesthood is unchangeable, so He ever lives to make intercession and is able to save to the uttermost those who come by Him (Hebrews 7:24-25). The worship of the Lamb and His throne go on for ever (Revelation 5:13; 22:3). Walk every era of the timeline, from John 1:1 to the throne, and He is there in each one.

teen.open: What never runs out? Jesus. He is the same yesterday, today, and forever (Hebrews 13:8), and His kingdom never ends.
teen.close: So the answer is Jesus. His reign, His prayers for you, and the worship of Him never run out. He was there before time, and He is there forever.

senior.open: The title asks what never runs out. The Word's answer is a Person: Jesus Christ, the same yesterday, today, and for ever (Hebrews 13:8), whose kingdom has no end (Luke 1:33).
senior.close: So what never runs out is He Himself, with His endless reign, His unchangeable priesthood that ever lives to intercede, and the worship of the Lamb before the throne. In every era of the line, He is there.
